summary: Introduces the ability for IS-IS to advertise link attributes of the individual member links of a Layer 2 bundle. Previously only the bundle as a whole was described, which is not enough for outside entities that want to steer traffic on specific physical links.

plainLanguage.summary: Several cables are tied together like one fat cable. This lets routers describe each thin cable inside, not just the bundle.

questions: what is an is-is l2 bundle member attributes tlv
subtitle: How IS-IS tells outside controllers about each physical link inside a Layer 2 bundle, not just the bundle as a whole.

tldr.problem: When the Layer 3 interface IS-IS runs on is a Layer 2 bundle such as a LAG, IS-IS only advertises attributes of the bundle as a whole. Outside entities that want to steer traffic onto individual member links have nothing to work with.
tldr.mechanism: A new IS-IS TLV (type 25) names a parent Layer 3 neighbor and then lists bundle members by Link Local Identifier, each group with its own link attributes. Two new sub-TLVs (41 and 42) carry one Adj-SID per member.
tldr.outcome: IS-IS can now advertise per-member bandwidth, delay, Adj-SIDs and similar attributes to external entities such as Path Computation Elements, without the bundle's members affecting the IS-IS decision process.

facts.label: Parent neighbor descriptor
facts.value: 7 octets system ID + pseudonode ID, plus 1 octet flags

today: RFC 8668 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the Adj-SID definitions in RFC 8667.

sections.title: Why Bundle Members Need Advertising
sections.content:
Some networks run an IS-IS adjacency over a Layer 2 bundle, for example a Link Aggregation Group (LAG). That keeps the routing protocol simple: with parallel links between two neighbors, IS-IS maintains one adjacency instead of many.

The catch is that IS-IS only describes the Layer 3 interface. Entities outside IS-IS, such as Path Computation Elements (PCEs), may want to control traffic on individual members of the bundle. To do that they need link attributes for each member, and this RFC supplies the means to advertise them.

The RFC is explicit about what it leaves out. It does not say which attributes will be advertised, what a default set is, how attributes are configured, how the advertisements are used, what effect they have on traffic, or how they reach the external entities.
sections.plainLanguage: A bundle hides the separate cables from the routing software. Planners outside the router want to see the separate cables, so this adds a way to describe them.

sections.title: The L2 Bundle Member Attributes TLV
sections.content:
The new L2 Bundle Member Attributes TLV has type 25. Much of its content is identical to what Extended IS Neighbor advertisements (TLVs 22 and 222) already carry, but the RFC uses a separate TLV on purpose, so that changes to member link attributes do not trigger unnecessary work in the ISO 10589 Decision Process.

The TLV starts with one Parent L3 Neighbor Descriptor: the neighbor's System ID plus pseudonode ID (7 octets) and a 1-octet flags field. Only one parent descriptor appears in a TLV. After it come one or more L2 Bundle Attribute Descriptors. Each has a 1-octet length, a 1-octet count of member descriptors, the members' Link Local Identifiers (4 octets each, as defined in RFC 4202) and then sub-TLVs.

Advertising a member implies that the link belongs to the named bundle and is operationally up. The advertisement MUST be withdrawn if the link goes down or leaves the bundle.
sections.plainLanguage: The message is a list. First it says which neighbor the bundle goes to. Then it lists the cables in the bundle by number, with notes about them.

sections.title: Telling Parallel Adjacencies Apart
sections.content:
A router can have several Layer 3 adjacencies to the same neighbor. The System ID alone then does not say which one the bundle belongs to, so extra information is needed.

The P flag in the parent descriptor's flags field controls this. When it is set to 1, exactly one of three sub-TLVs MUST immediately follow the flags: the IPv4 Interface Address (sub-TLV 6, from RFC 5305), the IPv6 Interface Address (sub-TLV 12, from RFC 6119) or the Link Local/Remote Identifiers (sub-TLV 4, from RFC 5307). When it is 0, none of them is present. The sub-TLV MAY be left out if no parallel adjacencies to the neighbor exist. Other flag bits MUST be zero when sent and ignored when received.
sections.plainLanguage: If you have two roads to the same town, you must say which road you mean. The P flag says an extra road label follows.

sections.title: Shared and Per-Member Attributes
sections.content:
Sub-TLVs inside a descriptor come in two classes. A shared attribute sub-TLV carries one copy of an attribute, such as link bandwidth, that applies to every bundle member listed in that descriptor. Only one copy of a given shared sub-TLV may appear; if several are present, all copies MUST be ignored.

That has a practical consequence: members listed together in one descriptor must share the same values for all the shared attributes. Members with different values go in separate descriptors. All existing sub-TLVs in the IANA registry for TLVs 22, 23, 141, 222 and 223 count as shared unless the RFC says otherwise.

The other class is attributes that are unique to each member. The new Adj-SID sub-TLVs are of this kind, as are the delay, loss and bandwidth-utilization sub-TLVs listed in the IANA table.
sections.plainLanguage: If three cables are all the same speed, you write the speed once. If one is faster, it gets its own line.

sections.title: Adjacency SIDs for Bundle Members
sections.content:
RFC 8667 defines sub-TLVs that advertise an Adjacency Segment Identifier (Adj-SID), an instruction telling forwarding to send traffic over a specific link, but each carries only one Adj-SID. Since each bundle member is expected to have its own Adj-SID in many deployments, this RFC defines two sub-TLVs that carry a whole set, one per member, in a single sub-TLV.

  • Sub-TLV 41, the L2 Bundle Member Adjacency Segment Identifier, is for a parent adjacency that is point-to-point.
  • Sub-TLV 42, the L2 Bundle Member LAN Adjacency SID, is for a parent LAN adjacency. It adds a 6-octet Neighbor System ID, because a router MAY advertise an Adj-SID for each member to each neighbor on the LAN.

Both start with a flags octet laid out as the bits F, an unused bit, V, L, S and P followed by unused bits, then a 1-octet weight used for load balancing (defined in RFC 8402). Flags and weight are shared by every member in the descriptor. F says whether the Adj-SID is for IPv4 or IPv6 encapsulation, and P marks a persistently allocated value. The unused bit is kept only to match the RFC 8667 layout: it SHOULD be sent as 0 and MUST be ignored on receipt.

After that comes one descriptor per member. With V and L both set, it is a 3-octet local label using the 20 rightmost bits. With both unset, it is a 4-octet index into the router's SID/label space. S set means the Adj-SID refers to a set of members and MAY be given to other members too.
sections.plainLanguage: Each cable gets its own ticket number that says send things down this exact cable. The new message hands out a whole stack of tickets at once.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA adds TLV 25, L2 Bundle Member Attributes, to the IS-IS TLV Codepoints registry. The registry of sub-TLVs for TLVs 22, 23, 141, 222 and 223 is renamed to include TLV 25 and gains a column showing which sub-TLVs may appear in TLV 25. The new sub-TLVs 41 and 42 are added with y for TLV 25 and n for all the others.

The column uses three values, and the RFC fills it in for every existing sub-TLV.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of message types gets new entries, plus a column saying which notes are allowed in the new message.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
The RFC argues that it introduces no new security issues. IS-IS has long advertised link attributes, and these advertisements are identical to those in RFC 4202, RFC 5305, RFC 8570 and RFC 8667, only associated with links inside a bundle.

The usual caveat applies: if an attacker can reach the physical links that carry IS-IS PDUs, attacks are possible. The RFC recommends IS-IS authentication as defined in RFC 5304 and RFC 5310 to prevent them.
sections.plainLanguage: Telling people about the separate cables is no riskier than telling them about the bundle. Locking the door with a password still helps.

sections.title: Worked Encoding Example
sections.content:
The appendix encodes two parallel adjacencies to a neighbor with System ID 1234.1234.1234.00. Adjacency 1 has local address 192.0.2.1 and four members; adjacency 2 has local address 192.0.2.2 and three members. Each adjacency needs its own TLV, so there are two TLVs.

Inside the first TLV, members 1 and 2 (1G) go in one descriptor and members 3 and 4 (10G) in another, because they have different bandwidth and bandwidth is a shared attribute. Each descriptor has a Maximum Link Bandwidth sub-TLV and an L2 Bundle Member Adj-SID sub-TLV. The second TLV needs only one descriptor, since all three of its members are 10G.
sections.plainLanguage: Two roads get two notes. On the first road, slow cables and fast cables are listed in separate groups. On the second, they are all fast, so one group is enough.
